title: Constance, 1414–1418
hookLine: three men claim to be pope, and a council ends the split

cards: A parish priest in those years could honestly not be sure who the pope was. One man in Rome claimed the office. Another, in Avignon in southern France, claimed it too.

Then a council at Pisa tried to fix things by electing a third, and the other two refused to step aside. Kingdoms lined up behind different men. It was a mess no one could pray their way out of alone.
Today's word is Constance, the German lakeside town where the bishops finally met to end it.

teach.b: First, the knot. Each claimant had cardinals, bishops and rulers behind him, and each said the others were the false ones. Ordinary Catholics wanted one shepherd and couldn't find him.
Then, the council gathers. The German king Sigismund pressed for it, and the claimant from the Pisa line called it. Bishops, abbots, theologians and princes came.
When that claimant saw where things were going, he slipped out of town in disguise.
He was brought back, and the council deposed him.

Next, the man in Rome. Gregory the Twelfth did something rare: he allowed the council to be formally called in his name, and then he resigned, letting go of the office so the Church could have one pope.

Catholic lists of the popes follow his line, and his resignation opened the door. The claimant in Avignon would not yield, and the council deposed him too, though he held out to the end with a few supporters.
Then the council elected one man, who took the name Martin the Fifth, and the split was over.
There's a hard shadow on this council, and it should be named: it also condemned the Czech preacher Jan Hus, who was burned at the stake.
Pope John Paul the Second later spoke of deep regret over his death. Paul asks the Ephesians, in the Douay-Rheims, to be "careful to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace."
At Constance, unity cost something: one man had to let go.

how: Catholics pray for the unity of the Church at Mass and in particular during the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity; the Council of Constance is remembered as the council that ended the Western Schism.

games.q: you're Gregory XII, the claimant in Rome. a council is gathering to end the split. what do you do?
o: refuse to recognize the council at all.
let the council be called in your name, then resign.
flee the city before it can act.
games.why: Gregory allowed the council to be formally convoked and then resigned, so the Church could have one pope.

practice: Bring to mind one split you know of, in a parish, a family, a group of friends, or between churches, and hold both sides in view for a few breaths without deciding who's right.

Then ask what one person would need to let go of for the knot to loosen, and whether that person could be you. If you pray, ask for the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace; if not, simply hold that unity in mind.

wordCard.voice: Constance. The council in a German lakeside town that ended the split of rival popes, with one resignation, two depositions and one election. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: three popes, then one. Sometimes unity comes back when one person lets go. Until tomorrow.
